incident_description:
The DreamNest is marketed and sold in the United States as a sleep product for infants. The company claims it has a pediatric approved 15 incline, follows AAP safety guidelines, and is designed to reduce SIDS risk.

However, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) 2022 Safe Sleep Guidelines and the Safe Sleep for Babies Act, infant sleep products must:
		Provide a firm, flat surface with an incline not greater than 10
		Not use straps, wraps, or positioners to secure babies in place
		Avoid marketing inclined products as safe for overnight sleep

The DreamNest contradicts these standards because:
	1.	It has a 15 incline, exceeding the safe maximum.
	2.	It includes a wrap/strap system to hold babies in place, which the AAP specifically warns against.
	3.	It is marketed as following AAP guidelines when, in fact, it does not.

Why This Matters:
This product may mislead parents into believing it is AAP-approved and legally compliant, when in reality its design characteristics (incline and restraint system) present suffocation and positional asphyxia risks that federal law and the AAP explicitly prohibit.

Requested Action:
		Investigate the DreamNests marketing and design for compliance with the Safe Sleep for Babies Act.
		Evaluate whether the products claims of AAP safety constitute false or misleading advertising.
		Take action to protect parents and infants if the product is found to be unsafe or falsely marketed.
justification: The product's design and marketing pose a risk of suffocation and positional asphyxia, which can lead to infant death, and the likelihood is possible given the product's non-compliance with safety standards.

incident_description:
We purchased a Pop N Go Tent Playpen  (1.0) made by California Beach Co. and have had it for a couple of years. For almost its entire life (99.9% of the time), it has been kept indoors in our childrens playroom. It has only been taken outside about three times in total.

On the most recent occasion, after bringing it back inside, I suddenly found black splinters and shiny fibers embedded in my hands. At first I did not know where they came from, but after inspecting the playpen, I discovered that one of the tent poles had fractured in a way similar to a greenstick break.

The fracture exposed raw fiberglass inside the pole. Either my hand touched the fractured area directly while moving the tent, or the break released fiberglass dust and fibers into the surrounding area, which I then contacted. This resulted in multiple fiberglass splinters all over my hands.

The injury was painful and required me to remove numerous fiberglass particles. While I was the one injured, this is a product designed to be around children. If one of my kids had touched the fractured pole or come into contact with the fibers, the consequences could have been far worse.

From my inspection, the inside of the pole appeared unusually dry, suggesting that the fiberglass may not have been properly bound with resin. This may have contributed to the pole breaking in a way that released hazardous fibers rather than failing in a safer manner.
justification: The incident resulted in painful fiberglass splinters requiring removal, indicating an injury (severity 3). The likelihood is rated as 3 (possible) given the product's design flaw and potential for similar failures.

Subject: Urgent Safety Concern Regarding Huggies Snug & Dry Diapers and Severe Red Burn Reaction

Dear Kimberly-Clark Team,

I am writing to report a recurring and deeply concerning issue involving your Huggies Snug & Dry Size 5 diapers. Our 15-month-old baby has experienced repeated severe diaper burns this week after we just opened a new box of diapers.  At first we were assuming this was just a rash. But upon closer inspection, we took note that this is obviously no rash. The  reactions occurred despite our careful hygiene practices including frequent diaper changes, avoiding wipes, and using warm baths to soothe the skin.

After researching online, we discovered multiple reports from other parents describing similar reactions allegedly linked to Huggies diapers:

1. Report of chemical burn-like rash from Huggies Little Movers [REDACTED]

2. Parent complaint about rash and raw skin after switching to new Huggies batch [REDACTED]

3. Class action alleging chemical burns from Huggies diapers [REDACTED]

To mitigate the burn, we applied [REDACTED] Butt Paste and inserted a double-layered paper towel between the diaper and our babys skin before putting our baby in the crib for the night.  When the baby woke up he did not urinate during the night as his diaper was dry.  But amazingly, the burn was 100% completely gone. This method led to rapid healing  overnight. Needless to say, I did not know there is a helpful visual guide that demonstrates this remedy when addressing rashes in general. 
[REDACTED]

But to reiterate my complaint, we were not dealing with the rash we were dealing with a reddish chemical burn appearance.

When we repeated the paper towel buffer method this morning, as the baby would obviously need to urinate, the paper towel interfered with urine absorption, and a new red spot appeared in an area not covered by the paper towel buffer. This observation occurred within 5 minutes after changing our baby's diaper from last night as we wanted to apply a new layer of paste. This suggests a possible reaction to the diaper material itself. Our ultimate solution at this point is to change to a different diaper product.

We respectfully request the following:

A formal investigation into this issue.  
Disclosure of all chemical components used in Huggies Snug & Dry diapers. 
Product recall.

We are also submitting a consumer product safety complaint via the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission:  
https://www.saferproducts.gov/

Sincerely,  
[REDACTED] 
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident describes a severe red burn reaction in a baby, indicating injury, and mentions multiple similar reports, suggesting possible occurrence.

incident_description:
I have a Storkcraft Santorini 5-in-1 Convertible crib and a [REDACTED] and Toddler Mattress. My baby just graduated to sleeping in the crib after learning to roll over so therefore the bassinet is no longer safe sleep. During her first night's sleep on the night of August 13th, 2025, she rolled over and got her arm caught between the mattress and crib slats. 

Thankfully she is room sharing with us so I woke up  hearing her coughing after struggling to roll back over. I found her laying on her stomach with her right arm trapped under her and left arm between the mattress and slats. The next morning on August 14th, 2025 I noticed the mattress didn't fit as snug as I believed it should. I pressed the mattress to the side and noticed just how large the gap is for her arm to fit. I did some research and found that the standard crib size, also known as a full-size crib, has interior dimensions of 28 inches in width by 52 3/8 inches in length, with a permissible variation of plus or minus 5/8 of an inch, according to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). This means a standard crib's dimensions are typically within the range of 27 3/8" to 28 5/8" wide and 51 3/4" to 53" long.

The Wayfair listing for this crib continuously states that it is a STANDARD size crib, that it will safely fit any standard size mattress, and it meets or exceeds ATSM and CPSIA standards. However, the dimensions of the product state it is " CRIB DIMENSIONS: Width (54.25 inches) x Depth (29.85 inches) x Height (35.83 inches)."

This means that the crib dimensions are a full 1.25 inches TOO LONG and 1.23 inches TOO WIDE. This much extra space leaves gaps around a standard crib mattress and poses a suffocation risk. My baby got stuck but I thankfully got to her BEFORE she tired of trying to free herself and something worse happened. 

The wayfair listing also states it's designed to fit any standard crib or toddler mattress but that is simply untrue because every mattress I have found (including the [REDACTED] ones they suggest, and the [REDACTED] one I have) fall within the dimension guidelines for safety so EVERY SINGLE MATTRESS will be TOO SMALL for this crib!

Length gap: ~0.94 per end
Width gap: ~0.93 per side

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission says any gap bigger than 2 fingers (about 1 inch) between the mattress and crib frame is unsafe. This crib would have just under an inch of space per side if the mattress stayed firmly in the center of the crib, which is right at the danger threshold - but it does NOT and the movements of baby easily moves the mattress further to one side over the other making a gap on one side over 1 inch and nearly TWO inches.

I'll be pursuing a full refund, replacement, and pushing for an immediate recall of this unsafe crib.
justification: The baby got her arm caught but was not injured, and the incident was resolved without harm.

incident_description:
On April 13, 2025, my 1-year-old son was using the walker when it unexpectedly flipped backward over a doorway threshold. He struck the back of his head on the floor, which led to a probable syncopal seizure and concussion. He received emergency medical attention.

On April 13, I initiated a return, and on April 14 I filed an Amazon A-to-Z Guarantee Claim and messaged the seller requesting manufacturer contact information. On April 16, I posted a detailed Amazon review documenting the injury. The seller refunded my purchase on April 27 without requesting the walker be returned. Amazon then closed my A-to-Z claim. I still retain the walker in its original condition.

On May 27, a pediatric neurologist evaluated my son and confirmed the incident was likely a probable syncopal seizure due to trauma. On June 12, he experienced a second seizure following a minor fall, which is possibly attributed to a lowered seizure threshold from the original head injury.

The product was advertised as anti-rollover yet failed under normal indoor conditions. The warranty phone number was disconnected, the seller has not provided any explanation or safety guidance, and the product has since been removed from Amazon with no recall or warning issued.

Injuries & Medical Treatment:
	Seizure and concussion after the April incident
	Emergency Room visit
	Pediatric neurology follow-up on May 27 (probable syncopal seizure)
	Second seizure on June 12; additional follow-up scheduled for August 29, 2025

Update 7/21/2025: Upon further inspection, I have discovered that the warning label attached to the walker does not refer to hazards associated with baby walkers. Instead, it appears to contain warnings related to changing tables ÃÂ which is not only misleading, but potentially a significant labeling error.

I am concerned that this walker may not meet federal labeling and safety standards under 16 CFR Part 1216. I have retained the walker and attached a photo of the mislabeled warning.
justification: The incident resulted in a seizure and concussion requiring emergency medical attention and follow-up care, indicating an injury (severity 3). The product's failure under normal conditions and mislabeling suggest a likely recurrence if used (likelihood 4).

On May 17th, 2023 around 6:20 pm, our 20 month old daughter was playing near an Evenflo adjustable wooden baby gate in our dining room. She was tossing toys over the baby gate into the kitchen. I was across the room from her and I noticed she would occasionally bite at the top of the baby gate after tossing over a toy. I didn't think too much of it as she wasn't doing it for very long. She was teething and put her mouth on everything, as babies and toddlers do.

She was standing next to and facing the baby gate and all of a sudden she let out a horrible scream as she fell away from the baby gate. She ran towards me with blood all over her face and neck. The baby gate was still standing, but had blood at the top near one of the metal clasps that holds the baby gate together. I knew she needed to go to the hospital right away.

Once we got her to a room at the hospital, we could see how bad her mouth was torn. The whole left side of her upper lip was ripped off, up the left side of her philtrum and away from her nose. Her cheek was torn down past the bottom of her mouth and there was another tear on her bottom lip. This exposed most of her top and bottom teeth on that side. The surgeon told us he would not be able to reattach the inch by inch section that was missing from her upper lip. There wasn't enough blood flow to it for it to be viable. He had to close her up as well as he could to prevent infection. After the surgery, the opening of her mouth was so small. She had a hard time eating, drinking, and speaking for a while.

Our daughter's lips were caught in the gap between one of the top metal clasps and the wooden gate panels. Her lips were pinched in the baby gate so tightly it caused significant tearing and loss of upper lip tissue and muscle. This baby gate was bought to help keep our baby safe from things she shouldn't get into. I would have never purchased this had I known this was a possibility.
justification: The incident resulted in severe injury to the child, including significant tearing and loss of upper lip tissue, requiring surgery and impacting her ability to eat, drink, and speak.

incident_description:
What happened?

We received a crib (Marley Crib in White/Natural, Model W4901, Serial Number HS0241402407, manufactured in 07/2024) as a gift from my sister when our son was 4 months old. At that time, we didnt use the crib because we already had one more suitable for younger infants. When our son turned 10 months old, we finally assembled and began using the Marley crib.

On the second day of use, we noticed that our son had scraped off paint from the top rail of the crib with his mouth. Like many babies at this stage, he has a natural tendency to bite and chew on things, especially crib rails. What concerned us most was that he has only one tooth, which means it took very little pressure to cause the paint to chip off and end up in his mouth.

This immediately raised serious safety concerns. We stopped using the crib right away. We also contacted our pediatrician the same day and waited hours to get a response. The pediatrician told us that as long as the paint flakes were small, it shouldnt be dangerous, but recommended routine lead testing at 12 months of age to be sure. Until then, theres no way to be fully certain if ingestion caused any harm.

After researching online, we were alarmed to find multiple reviews dating as far back as 2019 describing the same problembabies scraping and ingesting paint from the same crib model or brand. This shows that the issue is not isolated and may indicate a wider safety defect that hasnt been properly addressed by the manufacturer.

Who was using the product?

Our 10-month-old baby boy.

How was the product being used?

The crib was assembled and used as intendedfor our baby to sleep in.

Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product?

Yes, our son ingested paint chips from the crib. While there were no visible immediate symptoms, ingestion of paintespecially if containing any toxinsposes a serious risk to health. We are awaiting future test results to ensure there was no harm caused.

How did any injuries occur?

The injury occurred when the baby bit on the rail of the crib and scraped off paint into his mouth. The paint easily came off due to poor adhesion or low durability, despite the product being nearly brand new.
justification: The baby ingested paint chips, which constitutes an injury, and similar incidents have been reported multiple times, indicating a likely recurrence.

incident_description: We had used Philips Avent bottles and nipples with our daughter in 2021 and were very satisfied, so we chose them again for our exclusively bottle-fed newborn son without hesitation. We spent weeks trying to identify the cause and consulted  our pediatrician, who recommended a number of interventions like changing to a hypoallergenic formula, starting reflux medication, and ordering larger flow nipples (we tried flow 3 and 4). We also met with two different lactation consultants and both of them said there are known issues with new, re-designed  Avent nipples. We tested all of the ones we had at home and we found that many of the nipples regardless of flow size were dispensing little to no liquid at all. There was significant variability, even among nipples of the same size. Checking the one star reviews on Amazon for this product revealed that many others have experienced the same issue. Switching to a different bottle type resolved all issues immediately - feeding improved, reflux disappeared, and our son began thriving. I hope Philips Avent will investigate this issue thoroughly and implement better quality control to ensure other families do not endure the same hardship.

incident_description:
Philips Avent makes a baby bottle called "Natural Response." https://www.usa.philips.com/c-m-mo/baby-bottles/natural-response

These bottles come with nipples rated for milk flow for babies of certain ages. You can see those ratings on their Amazon store page https://www.amazon.com/Philips-Natural-Newborn-SCF651-43/dp/B07N976C6R.

A few years ago Philips Avent redesigned their nipples to have a new design with a spiral cut pattern in the top of the nipple. These new nipples no longer allow milk to flow. The nipple sizes 0, 1, and 2 are not usable by babies. Milk does not come out of the bottle. The nipples rated for babies of certain ages do not allow those babies to drink.

In my own experience, I received a Philips Avent Natural glass baby bottle as a gift with a Flow 2 rated nipple. According to Philips, a Flow 2 is appropriate for a 1month+ year old. I tried bottle feeding my 6 day old baby with this nipple. There was no milk flow at all. It took me a while to realize the baby was not getting any milk. My child had a lower than expected weight gain. It is also very distressing to try to feed a screaming infant at 4am without having access to any other bottles.

I have contacted Philips Avent support who claim I have a defective bottle. However I highly doubt this is case. The nipple flow sizes 0, 1 and 2 no longer allow milk flow after the redesign. There are thousands of 1 star reviews of the nipples that say exactly this, including many reports of lower weight in babies. A small sample of reviews that match my exact experience:

> Nipple doesnt provide enough flow to a newborn. Baby gets more tired trying to pull milk though than what is actually being produced. Called advent and they sent me replacement nipples. Same result. Would not recommend. Baby lost weight as of a result.

> Please do not buy. We bought because my son was struggling to gain weight and we were supplementing with formula. Caused days of distress as he would take NOTHING from the bottle even though he was sucking on it. These are known to not let any flow through. We jumped straight to size 3 for nipples because 1 and 2 were so bad.

>  Big mistake. First I bought the same number as the one she took to. No indication that they changed them other than inclusion of response in the name. She screamed and screamed because the flow was too low.

There are thousands of these reviews on the store page https://www.amazon.com/Philips-Natural-Newborn-SCF651-43/dp/B07N976C6R

Philips Avent refuses to take action despite the pervasiveness of this issue for years.
justification: The incident involves babies experiencing lower weight gain due to the inability to feed, which constitutes an injury.

incident_description:
I am writing to report a safety concern regarding a children's playpen that tested positive for lead content. 

Upon advice from our pediatrician, I used a lead testing kit after finding that my 12 month had elevated lead levels of 8.6. The product in question is a playpen, still currently available for purchase on Amazon. The metal threads on the playpen bolts were the specific components that tested positive for lead, raising serious safety concerns. I used three different brands of testing kits. 

The playpen was used by my child as a safe space for play and rest. The presence of lead in the metal threads creates a significant risk of lead exposure, particularly for infants and toddlers who may come into contact with or mouth these components. It is very easy for him to remove those bolts. 

However, the potential for lead poisoning is alarming, particularly given the elevated lead levels already detected in my child's system. This exposure to lead poses severe long-term health risks to young children, including developmental delays and cognitive impairments.

I urge the CPSC to investigate this matter promptly to ensure the safety of other consumers and prevent further lead exposure through this product.

Thank you for your attention to this critical issue.
justification: The child has elevated lead levels, indicating injury, and the playpen's lead exposure risk is likely for other users.

I purchased the "Simple Serve (TM) Fast Bottle Warmer" by The First Years on 10/19/2024. The bottle warmer comes with a vial with numbers 1 through 5 marked on it. The instructions indicate if wanting to warm a 4 oz bottle of thawed breast milk to fill the vial to the 4 line, pour the water in the warmer, then press the on button to turn it on. The device will turn off when the bottle is warm. I used the bottle warmer for 6 days and found the breastmilk in the bottle was way too hot to feed a baby when warmed based on instructions. Thankfully, I tested the milk temperature against my wrist before feeding my baby. 

Further issues with this product are that the device does not turn off. The "power button" does not turn off. So if a caregiver is warming the bottle and determines it is warm enough and there is still water in the warmer, the device must be unplugged or it stays on, continuing to steam water. I unplugged the device but when I plug it back in to warm another bottle, it automatically turns on. 

I consider this device defective and unsafe. The instructions are inaccurate and insufficient. Milk warmed according to direction is too hot to serve a baby. The device cannot be turned off with the power button. Any attempts to adjust the water amount to find a better quantity to warm the milk adequately resulted in me having a bottle warmer with remaining water in it that if I forgot to unplug, would continue to boil and emit hot steam. 

I think this product should be recall due to the inadequate instructions as well as the inability to turn it off. 

I purchased the product at the Augusta Maine Target store on 10/20/24 and returned it on 10/29/24 with a reason for the return as "Defective."
justification: The device overheats milk and cannot be turned off without unplugging, posing a burn risk to babies, but no injury was reported as the caregiver tested the temperature.

These substances can be particularly hazardous for young children, whose developing bodies are more susceptible to environmental toxins. Potential Non-compliance with Safety Standards: Given the nature of the product as a child's crib, the presence of a strong chemical odor raises concerns about the compliance of the product with safety standards for children's furniture, especially regarding non-toxic finishes and materials. Actions Taken: The crib has been left in a well-ventilated room to air out since its assembly. Despite these measures, the strong odor persists. Pottery Barn was contacted, and they replaced the crib with the same model of crib, but the overwhelming smell was present with this crib as well so we insisted that they take the crib back and issue a refund. Another crib was purchased from a different retailer and it has no smell or issue.
 Requested Actions: - Investigation into the Chemical Composition of the Paint/Finish: We request that PBK investigates the chemical composition of the paint or finish used on the Kendall crib to  ensure it is safe for children and complies with relevant safety standards. The description of the crib on PBK website says that it is "GREENGUARD GOLD CERTIFIED
Our GREENGUARD Certifies products contribute to cleaner indoor air." That cannot be possible as this crib has a horrible unsafe smell and has to be false advertising.
 - Remedial Measures: If the product is found to be unsafe, we request immediate action to rectify the issue, which could include a recall, replacement, or refund. - Public Notification: We suggest that Pottery Barn inform consumers who have purchased this product about potential risks and the steps being taken to address the issue.

incident_description:
My 10-month old son choked on and nearly swallowed a metal bolt that came with an infants toy play gym, that had come loose on its own due to the unreliable (and in my carpenter's opinion, incompatible) hardware that was included in the assembly. He was suddenly choking near the play gym and I had to throw him upside down and perform back thrusts to dislodge it from his airway. Luckily after several tries it came out and he could breathe again. 
I am an amateur carpenter, so I know nuts and bolts so to say, and upon inspection after the incident I can tell that the included nut and barrel bolt used to fasten the arms of the play gym are not compatible for a tight connection. This is because even when threaded completely into the nut, the bolt still wriggles slightly in place. This means that there is space in the threads and so it lacks the tension required to normally keep hardware from loosening on its own, which it will easily do from even light handling/movement such as a child pulling on the dangling rope accessories, or from a parent moving the gym around. I had fervently tightened the included hardware when I first assembled the gym per the instructions, and it only took a few weeks for the bolt pieces to pop back out and nearly choke my child to death. I was extremely lucky to have intervened before it could have been worse, had he swallowed it completely or asphyxiated, and I hope this company will warn other parents who already have his play gym about the hardware and also work to replace the pieces with ones that won't unthread themselves and become choking hazards.
justification: The child choked on a metal bolt but was successfully treated, indicating an injury was narrowly avoided.

Then she realized that my daughter was choking and saw that the whole pacifier was inside of her mouth. She attempted to remove the pacifier with her finger  without success as the pacifier was pulled down her throat from the crying and sucking. She immediately called 911 and they took my daughter to the emergency room where they sedated her and was able to remove the whole pacifier from her throat (photo attached). Luckily, the pacifier was lodged in her throat in such a way that it wasn't fully blocking her airway. She suffered throat trauma, lacerations, bruises and emotional trauma. She was hospitalized for almost two days.
justification: The child suffered throat trauma, lacerations, bruises, and emotional trauma, requiring hospitalization, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The incident involved a pacifier, a common item in daycare settings, making such occurrences possible (likelihood 3).

incident_description: My 11-month-old granddaughter (weigh at the time of the incident - 20 pounds) was using the Baby Trends Lil Snooze Deluxe II Nursery Center when the side rail collapsed causing her to fall and hit her head on the bottom of the play yard. Thankfully she did not fall out onto the floor and hurt herself. I contacted Amazon where I bought it and was directed to Baby Trends who manufactured it for support under the warranty. When I emailed the manufacturer, I was told that the reason the lock released is because of her weight. The lock did not simply release. It completely BROKE. If only 20 pounds of pressure can cause a safety latch to become dislodged or break on a product that has a maximum weight limit of 30KG or 66.14 pounds meant to keep growing infants and toddlers safe, that is a major safety concern. I was advised by the manufacturer to completely collapse the unit to re lock the rail, which I did before I even contacted them, and the rail will not lock no matter what I do. It didn't just unlatch, the lock broke.
justification: The infant fell but did not sustain any injuries, indicating an incident without injury. The lock mechanism failure suggests a likely recurrence under similar conditions.

incident_description: My 15 month old son was drinking out of a Glass and Sprout Ware Sip & Straw cup today, made by Green Sprouts, that is advertised as being safe for babies 6+ months old. He dropped the cup, as babies do constantly, then took a drink out of it. I noticed milk dripping from the bottom of the cup and took it away, and saw that the glass liner inside the plastic outer coating was broken into sharp shards. My son was using the sippy cup as it was intended and we are not sure if there are any injuries yet from ingesting slivers of glass yet or now. We have to watch him for symptoms of coughing, vomiting, and blood in his stool, and if there is he needs to go to the emergency room likely for emergency surgery to remove any shards and to stop internal bleeding. The pediatrician was contacted immediately and gave instructions on what symptoms to look for, and what to do if any of the symptoms show up.
justification: The incident involved a broken glass liner in a sippy cup, but no immediate injuries were observed. However, potential ingestion of glass shards poses a risk of injury, which is being monitored.

However, this morning, our 4 week old son wiggled and rolled in his bassinet to the edge where he could have suffocated on the product side. His face was beside the solid fabric panel on the zip-down part without mesh. His face was millimeters away from smothering. We've noticed the product slightly leans to the side of the bassinet meant to go against the bed. We checked for proper assembly and it still leans. When searching online about this concern, several other consumers reported this same problem in their reviews on [REDACTED]. The solid fabric panel and the slight lean are deadly!

incident_description:
Munchkin Float Foldable Baby and Toddler High Chair, White, Unisex
This product is not safe for children, the straps do not stay tight allowing babies to move into positions that could either make them choke on their food or get loose from the harness. So far I have complied at least 5+ reviews from various websites about this same problem so it does not seem to be a one-off problem. My child is currently 10 months old and has had a problem with this since he was 8 months old. I thought it was just me but now I realize it is not, I reached out to the company and they acted like they had never heard this before but they have commented on the reviews. It is stated that this is safe to use for ages 6-36 months, but even after tightening the straps after each use it is still not enough there is far too much space between the seat and the tray. In one feeding he goes from sitting up straight to almost laying down just from normal moving He is not doing anything that should make the straps loose. I am afraid that this could seriously cause a choking incident and/or a child getting loose.
justification: The product's faulty straps pose a risk of choking or injury to children, as evidenced by multiple reports and the parent's experience.

incident_description: I recently purchased and assembled a Halo BassiNest Glide Sleeper (https://www.halosleep.com/halo-bassinest-glide-sleeper). My daughter was born 3 days ago, and we came home from the hospital today. When I placed her in the bassinet, I noticed that she had a tendency to roll onto one side. This is highly unusual, as she is far too young to have acquired this developmental milestone. I took out a leveler and confirmed that the bassinet is tilted to one side, which causes the baby to roll onto one side when placed in it. This is highly concerning as infants rolling onto their side (and from there, to their stomachs) is a known risk factor for Sudden Infant Death Syndrome.
justification: The bassinet's tilt poses a risk for Sudden Infant Death Syndrome, a severe potential outcome.

incident_description: I purchased a convertible Sorelle crib in 2008 for twins I was expecting. Sadly, I lost them due to preterm labor. The crib was never assembled and stated in its box until 2018 when we were expecting a baby boy. He used the crib for 3 years, converting it to each stage of growth as he needed it. Since it was so mamy years, the original cherry color was not available,  not a huge concern. When it was being assembled,  of course it seemed as it wasnt going to work. Fast forward to the end- there literally is a 7 inch gap after putting the mattress on it. I had to put the crib mattress in the hole to the floor so it can be used. My son was devoted to sleeping in his new bed, there was no other way. Also, the wood colored blocks that were sent in kit stick out and are not flush with the rails. incident_description: On January 17, 2024, my 13 month daughter was touching a Fisher Price Sunnyside Snail Baby Bouncer at daycare when she got her right index finger stuck in the product.  When she pulled her finger away to get it un-stuck, she almost amputated her right index fingertip with a very deep laceration.  We took her to the [REDACTED] Hospital emergency room where they had to use a finger tourniquet to stop the bleeding.  She ended up receiving 4 stiches in her right fingertip under sedation from a pediatric orthopedic hand surgeon.  Fortunately, there was no fracture and the tendons, ligaments, and arteries were intact and not damaged.  But in her 5-day follow-up appointment with the pediatric orthopedic hand surgeon, they stated if she had been an adult this laceration was deep enough that it would have resulted in a fingertip amputation.
justification: The incident resulted in a very deep laceration requiring medical intervention, including stitches and sedation, indicating a significant injury.

incident_description:
I purchased a personalized bear busy board from Kindly Toys for my 10mo son for Christmas. This is not a safe toy for babies and toddlers. 

First off, the puzzle pieces that are personalized for your child's name are choking hazards. Upon more careful review, their terms and conditions even acknowledge that the "I" and "J" are choking hazards so they are supposed to be attached, the "I" on ours was absolutely not attached and I would advise that other letters including "L", "E" and "S" are also choking hazards for small children that are prone to put everything in their mouth. We had to pull all of the puzzle pieces off immediately once he received this gift. 

Second, my 10mo son was easily able to pull the sticks with balls loose - they are not securely attached and these balls are extremely hazardous. Even while supervising his play, these 9 small balls scattered everywhere when he pulled on the sticks and a couple of them were hard to locate, which was very concerning. He honestly hasn't played much with this toy and this was the first time he really engaged with it which is especially concerning because it means the sticks just aren't securely fastened at all. Thankfully there were no injuries as I was supervising him and immediately got him out of the room until I could locate each of these small wooden balls. I wanted to report this as I worry about more serious incidents occurring for other families unless there is more rigorous toy safety testing for this company.
justification: The incident involved potential choking hazards and loose parts, but no actual injury occurred due to supervision.

incident_description: We installed a Perma Retractable Baby Gate on our stairs for our 9 month old daughter who was becoming mobile. I put the gate up, so that I could good laundry and within 30 seconds of walking away, I heard multiple thumps. I walked to our stairs to see my daughter half way down the stairs, with the gate still completely closed. As Im trying to get over the gate, she rolled the rest of the way down the stairs. She can not pull up well enough to go over this, so the only possiblity is that this product is defective and has enough give to let a small child underneath, providing me with no peace of mind that a gate should provide. We took her to the ER and thankfully she was ok, but this could have been prevented if the product worked effectively and another child could not be so lucky.
justification: The child was injured by falling down the stairs due to a defective gate, requiring an ER visit, but thankfully no serious harm occurred.

The Graco Benton 5-in-1 Convertible Crib is designed as a multipurpose crib that can be transformed into different types of beds for children. It is intended to be a long-lasting piece of furniture for a child's room.

The intensity of the smell is such that it causes discomfort to adults, making it difficult to stay in the same room as the product for more than a few minutes.

Health and Safety Risk: The strong paint-like smell suggests the possibility of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) or other potentially harmful chemicals being present. These substances can be particularly hazardous for young children, whose developing bodies are more susceptible to environmental toxins.
Potential Non-compliance with Safety Standards: Given the nature of the product as a child's crib, the presence of a strong chemical odor raises concerns about the compliance of the product with safety standards for children's furniture, especially regarding non-toxic finishes and materials.

Actions Taken:
The crib has been left in a well-ventilated room to air out since its assembly.
Despite these measures, the strong odor persists.

- Investigation into the Chemical Composition of the Paint/Finish: We request that Graco investigates the chemical composition of the paint or finish used on the Benton 5-in-1 Convertible Crib to ensure it is safe for children and complies with relevant safety standards.

incident_description:
Pura Stainless knowingly sold Lead-contaminated children's products through at least 2018. There was no recall. These products are still in use in homes today. Summary / Overview:

In 2017 and 2018 - and possibly later - Pura Stainless continued to sell high-Lead-content insulated stainless steel Pura Kiki baby bottles after learning of the following issue with their product: multiple documented instances of product failure resulting in child-accessible Lead at very high levels (as much as 800,000 ppm) in one component ÃÂ far in excess of the CPSIA Lead-content ban for Lead in children's products (limiting Lead in substrates to 100 ppm.) Pura's sales of Lead-contaminated children's product on store shelves (virtual and brick and mortar) and distribution from warehouse inventory continued after the company stated (in writing to customers - see below) that they had begun to manufacture a Lead-free version of the product. Lead-contaminated versions of this product continued to be sold through at least 2018, and may have been sold as late as 2019 (possibly even later, until Lead-contaminated inventory was exhausted). These unsafe and illegal Lead-contaminated baby bottles are still in use in homes across the United States today in 2023, as no voluntary recall was ever announced by the manufacturer. Separately, [REDACTED] knowingly continued to allow their certification to be used on the packaging of (and marketing for) these products ÃÂ after learning that the products were in violation of the CPSIA due to unsafe levels of Lead. See attached PDF for full report which your website did not accept in text form.

We have published correspondence from Pura Kiki dated July 7, 2018 where they admit that they are continuing to sell their (older) Lead-contaminated stock (see website) despite having been directly made aware of the Lead issue in 2017.
FOUR) Compounding Factor: Product Durability / Intended Duration of Use: A primary compounding factor with this product is that it was marketed and sold as an item that can be used throughout a child's entire early childhood. As a result, if a parent bought this Lead-contaminated bottle to use for their newborn in 2018 or 2019 (or even in earlier years) the intention - by design, and in confirmed practice) was that the child would still be using the product - continuously - when they were four or five or six years old. We have found this to be the case - see point number nine below. Their slogan, "Baby GrowsÃÂBottle Evolves" underscores this concern [see attached image with their marketing language relevant to this product]. In support of any investigation you may undertake in this matter, we have a full timeline indicating the company's knowledge of the issue - and the fact that they continued to sell Lead-contaminated bottles, in spite of this knowledge -  on our website ([REDACTED])
FIVE) Compounding Factor: Fraudulent / Misleading Packaging with Made Safe Certification Language: The company used and continues to use language including the following phrases (which would indicate to the consumer that the product is Lead-free): "Made Safe Certified"; "Eco-progressive"; "Toxin-Free"; "Kids Safety and Sustainability First"...
SIX) Date Issue First Reported by [REDACTED]:  April / May 2017
SEVEN) Dates of Documented (saved) Communication Thread with CPSC about this product: We have several saved communications with the CPSC about this product specifically and this issue in general from July 2018 (see our website for full communication thread). There were also earlier communications about this issue but we did not save copies. After this exchange from July of 2018, we never received a response or determination of next steps. These communications were with the following parties: [REDACTED], [REDACTED] and [REDACTED]. We were told on July 30, 2018 that [REDACTED] would get back to us. We never heard back from anyone after this communication about this issue.
EIGHT) Date of Follow Up Letter to CPSC (sent to CPSC through former CPSC official as we had not received any response to our previous communications):  December 2021 (see our website for full communication).
NINE) 2023 Issue With This Product: [REDACTED] is a small business that does in-home visits with families of Lead-poisoned children around the country. This year (in the first 7 months of 2023) we have worked with several families who had a confirmed Lead-contaminated version of this product still in use in their home. There have been two common scenarios: #1) a child who had the bottle as an infant is now using the bottle at 4, 5 or 6 years old; and #2) the family has had a second or third child since they purchased this bottle 4 or 5 or 6 years ago, and they are now using the bottle (again) for their youngest infant. There is also a concern for these bottles (due to the promised durability of the product) to be handed down from one family to another. Each of these scenarios creates the opportunity for these bottles to poison children for years into the future, which is why we are demanding an investigation and recall of these bottles now, even though the company states that the current version of their products no longer use Lead to create their vacuum seal [they claim this is true for versions manufactured since mid-2018 (in a written response when pressed on the subject by a customer who also happened to be a reader of our posts, and forwarded that communication to us)].

The locking mechanism that sets the width of this gate is poorly designed and unsafe (I have designed guarding a in industrial settings myself) and I did indeed doubt the design when I saw it. Over the last day IÃÂve had to reset this stop multiple times. After the insistent IÃÂve also secured this stop with a screw. Fortunately today I was with my daughter and was able to save her. However some one else may not be so lucky. I implore safety first to issue a recall on this gate and address the two issues before returning this gate to market.

URGENT: POTENTIAL FIRE HAZARD

Graco soothe-n-sway-lx [Graco swing] (model number: 2140066) with (date of manufacture: 2022/08/12) smokes and is a potential fire hazard.

When I plugged my wife's breast pump (popular model) power adapter (12 volts - 2 amps) into said Graco swing which has a power adapter (5 volts - 2 amps), said Graco swing's motor smoked to the point where it could have caught on fire.

Said breast pump and Graco Swing use power adapters with the same size and shape of "female barrel jack" [barrel jack].

Many parents have a breast pump and Graco swing.  it is easy to place the wrong power adapter's female  barrel jack into the other unit's male power socket.  While this may be user error, Graco's electrical engineers should have put safety precautions in place.

I have not looked at the board as of yet.  I feel that it could be a power supply issue with the board.

The best safety precaution would have been to include a voltage regulator on the control board to step down the supplied 12 volts to the correct 5 volts that is needed for the Graco swing.

Another safety precaution that could have been placed on the control board would be a fuse (standard blown out, thermal reset, manual reset).

It seems that there are no safety precautions for the board and/or motor when inputting more than 5 volts, when considering that the motor burned out when applying 12 volts.

I have contacted Graco's customer service center.  I asked if there was a recall on the unit, and I was told there was not.  I explained the issue above multiple times to customer service.  I asked to speak with someone to go over the possible recall, and I was denied.  The  customer representative "[REDACTED]" stated that the phone calls are recorded, if you would like to request them for this report.

Let me know if you need me to clarify this report, or need more information.
justification: The incident involved smoking and a potential fire hazard, but no injury or death was reported.

On a recent visit to New York while staying at [REDACTED] Hotel we had the most frightening experience of our lives by using one of your cribs. 


I canÃÂt express how damaging this experience has been to our lives. We came away from the incident with a deep seated fear for the well being of our child and children in general that will linger, likely for the rest of our lives. 



Here's what happened:

We checked into [REDACTED] New York on the afternoon of May 16th this last month. I jostled the crib aggressively and while it had more play than a typical crib it seemed to be structurally sound, at least in my jetlagged brain at the moment. 


The morning of May 20th however was a different story. At about 5:30am our nanny who was sleeping on the bed next to [REDACTED] heard a crash and woke up. The floor of his crib had collapsed and he had slid down into the gap crated between the mattress and long sides of the crib, pinning him in place. These cribs are not appropriate for hotel use. They require diligent reassably each time that obviously cannot be ensured by whatever hotel staff is doing that work.

Further, this is a tremendously flawed and dangerous design. Competing cribs of similar, foldable design simply have hinges rather than removable parts so they can't be assembled without critical safety features in place. 
To solely rely upon warning labels and an instruction manual is immensely negligent. 

I urge your company to immediately recall these cribs and correct their design flaws before any child is injured or worse.
I've filed an "unsafe product report" with the Consumer Products Safety Commission. 


I hope you do the right thing. If not, please consider this note to be discoverable upon legal review. 


Sincerely, [REDACTED]

incident_description:
CPSC VIOLATION REPORT
Saturday - February 4, 2023

Glass baby bottles manufactured under the brand Lansinoh by the company Pigeon Corporation (based in in Japan) and sold in stores in the United States and via online vendors (including through Amazon dot com) have tested positive for unsafe levels of Lead in the exterior decorative painted markings   / logo markings and measurement markings. This is for ALL models and sizes of glass Lansinoh bottles manufactured and sold by Lansinoh through as recently as early-2022, and likely later.

CPSC INFORMED DATE

I originally informed the CPSC of this issue (through e-mails to administrators via a friend of [REDACTED] who is affiliated with the CPSC) on December 20, 2021. We did not file a formal violation report at that time because previous violation reports filed by [REDACTED] for Lead-contaminated childrenÃÂs items had not been responded to or acted upon by the CPSC (under the previous administration), and we wanted to see if approaching the CPSC through different channels could result in a response (given the urgency of the concern).

Alas, we did not receive any response from the CPSC after these communications were forwarded about this matter [I understand that in the past 6 years your ability to take action has been severely restricted, and a consequent backlog may be the likely cause of the lack of action on this issue]. 

Given the CPSCÃÂs encouraging recent quick response to members of the [REDACTED] community filing a violation report in response to our findings of the Lead-contaminated Insulate Stainless Steel Baby Bottles / Sippy Cups manufactured by [REDACTED], we decided it might be a good time to formally submit this violation report for the Lansinoh Lead-painted glass baby bottles [and several other products that we have not yet heard back from the CPSC on - regarding previously-communicated violations]. It is for this reason we are filing this report now (in February of 2022), ÃÂ despite it now constituting ÃÂoldÃÂ news [again we first confirmed the paint on these bottles was high-Lead paint (and reported this publicly at that time on the [REDACTED] website) back in December of 2021.]

COMPANY INFORMED DATE: 

[REDACTED] first reported this issue on our website (please do not redact our business name and website from your public filing of this report) [REDACTED] dot com on December 19, 2021. Lansinoh  / Pigeon was made aware of this problem shortly after that. Lansinoh responded to our findings on February 24, 2022 and so has been aware of these findings at least as of February of 2022. 

FAILURE OF COMPLIANCE WITH DUTY TO REPORT:

To our knowledge - since the time the company (Lansinoh / Pigeon) was made aware of this issue (the illegal levels of Lead on the paint of their glass baby bottles), Lansinoh has not made any public statements to customers about the issue, nor have they issued a voluntary recall on the product nor did they self-report the violation to the CPSC that we are aware of (as is required by law when a company learns of a CPSIA violation in a product they manufacture that is intended for use by children.) 

We are referring to the self-reporting requirement noted on this CPSC link:
https://www.cpsc.gov/Business--Manufacturing/Recall-Guidance - under the ÃÂDuty To ReportÃÂ tab: 


ÃÂIf you are a manufacturer, importer, distributor, and/or retailer of consumer products, you have a legal obligation to immediatelyÃÂ reportÃÂ the following types of information to the CPSC:
A defective product that could create a substantial risk of injury to consumers;
A product that creates an unreasonable risk of serious injury or death;
A product that fails to comply with an applicable consumer product safety rule or with any other rule, regulation, standard, or ban under the CPSA or any other statute enforced by the CPSC;
An incident in which a child (regardless of age) chokes on a marble, small ball, latex balloon, or other small part contained in a toy or game and that, as a result of the incident, the child dies, suffers serious injury, ceases breathing for any length of time, or is treated by a medical professional; and
Certain types of lawsuits. (This applies to manufacturers and importers only and is subject to the time periods detailed in Sec. 37 of the CPSA.)
Failure to fully and immediately report this information may lead to substantialÃÂ civilÃÂ orÃÂ criminalÃÂ penalties. ÃÂ CPSC staffÃÂs advice is "when in doubt, report.ÃÂ
We hope you use this measure (the allowance for civil and criminal penalties in this matter) to the fullest extent possible to discourage Lansinoh / Pigeon and other glass baby bottle manufacturers from painting their baby bottles with high-Lead paint.


DECEPTIVE MARKETING: 

These glass Lansinoh-brand bottles are manufactured, marketed and sold with the intention that they be used by the very youngest babies as a ÃÂbeneficialÃÂ alternative for mothers who are also breastfeeding their babies. Given the fact that these glass Lansinoh bottles are painted with high-Lead -content paint this is particularly deceptive marketing. From advertising for these products: Statement #1) ÃÂGREAT FOR NURSING MOMS- These breastfeeding bottles with NaturalWave Nipples are clinically proven to reduce nipple confusion so babies can switch back and forth between the breast and bottleÃÂ and Statement #2) ÃÂPREMIUM DURABLE GLASS- Made from premium borosilicate glass, these sturdy baby bottles are heat and thermal shock resistant. They're also BPA and BPS freeÃÂ

CURRENT 90 PPM LIMIT IN COATINGS: 

The CPSIA of 2008 requires that any component of a product manufactured for use by children should not have paint or coatings on that product that test positive for levels of 90 ppm Lead or higher; the painted logo and measurement markings on the glass Lansinoh bottles (painted with light purple / lavender colored paint on the exterior of their glass bottles) consistently tests positive for Lead at levels of 3,500 ppm and higher. This is especially concerning because it is the area of the bottle that would be touched and held by the infant for self-feeding purposes. This concern is compounded by the fact that babies often suck their hands / put their hands in their mouth (at any time, but especially likely and including after holding a bottle for a feeding, with no hand washing by the parent in-between.) The paint on these bottles also tested positive for traces of two known carcinogens: Cadmium (50 +/- 3 ppm) and Antimony (17 +/- 5 ppm)

INSTRUMENTATION USED FOR TESTING

The Lead levels in the paint on these products as reported by [REDACTED] were determined using a freshly-calibrated Niton XL3T XRF instrument testing in Consumer Goods mode, by a trained, certified, and experienced operator. [It is our understanding that this is the exact instrumentation used by the CPSC to screen consumer goods for unsafe levels of Lead.]

NO SAFE LEVEL OF LEAD: 

As you know, all Federal agencies agree that there is no safe level of Lead exposure for children. There is no defensible reason for a company to manufacture baby bottles with Lead-painted coatings in the current decade (especially considering that Lead-free alternatives are readily available). There is therefore no defensible reason for the CPSC to not take immediate action on this issue.

CPSIA VIOLATION: 

This is an egregious violation of the CPSIA of 2008, especially as the customers who purchase these bottles to feed their infants are specifically purchasing them because they are advertised to be a healthy, safer, more environmentally-friendly choice than plastic bottles.

ISSUE SPECIFICALLY LIMITED TO GLASS BOTTLES: 

Lansinoh also manufactures plastic baby bottles ÃÂ however, their plastic bottles are not impacted by this concern (the painted logos / decorations and measurement markings on the Lansinoh plastic bottles are not painted with Lead paint.)

[REDACTED] RECALL AS PRECEDENT: 

As a precedent for demanding a recall for these products, I will remind you of the recall the CPSC announced on July 28, 2022 (in response to a violation report submitted by [REDACTED] on June 16, 2021) for the glass [REDACTED] brand baby bottles (manufactured in Germany) which had decorations and measurement markings (gray and white painted stars with white logo) similarly painted with high Lead-paint.

TOY RECALL AS PRECEDENT:

Another precedent for this recall is the [REDACTED] plastic toy guns recalled on August 19, 2020 where it was ÃÂonlyÃÂ the decorative sticker / logo marking on the toy that tested positive for high levels of Lead. The level of Lead found in the [REDACTED] guns was approximately 2,761 ppm, significantly below the level of Lead found in the paint on these glass Lansinoh brand baby bottles.  The concern for Lead painted glass baby bottles should be treated with at least equal - if not greater - import and urgency (in terms of the CPSCÃÂs response to this violation report in initiating a recall), given the demographic of young children using the baby bottles and the increased relative potential for harm as compared to the potential harm that may be caused by a logo marking sticker on a [REDACTED] gun.)

LIKELY CORPORATE RESPONSE TO THIS REPORT: 

Separately, the manufacture of these baby bottles (Lansinoh / Pigeon) may assert (in their response to this CPSIA violation report) that the high-Lead paint on the outside of their glass baby bottles is ÃÂnot ÃÂmigratableÃÂ LeadÃÂ or ÃÂnot ÃÂbio-availableÃÂ LeadÃÂ and they may also assert that these bottles ÃÂcomply the required leach-testing standards for Lead at the time of manufacture". Unfortunately, these assertions (and possible defenses that may be raised by the company) are irrelevant ÃÂ not only when looking at CPSIA Lead-content limits in coatings for items intended for use by children, but also when one takes into account the ÃÂnormal use as intendedÃÂ for glass baby bottles: glass baby bottles are frequently washed in hot water with detergents; sterilized in boiling water or sterilized in a steam bath. All of those activities are normal and anticipated use of baby bottles, and all of those activities can result in the wear, deterioration and increased bio-availability of the high levels of Lead in the paint on the surface of these bottles - paint in an area right where babies put their hands when holding the bottles. The company specifically states in their advertising: ÃÂEASY TO USE AND CLEAN- These dishwasher safe baby bottles only have four pieces and can easily be cleaned and reassembled as often as needed.ÃÂ


NO EVIDENCE THAT THE PROBLEM HAS BEEN REMEDIED

[REDACTED] has searched online on the Lansinoh website, the CPSC website and elsewhere and has not yet been able to find any evidence that any recall was initiated or ordered, nor any evidence that Lansinoh has switched to Lead-free paints on their glass bottles since we made them aware of this concern [they may have switched to Lead-free paints since we alerted them of the issue, but we have seen no evidence suggesting that].  Even if they have switched/do [at some point in the future] quietly switch to a Lead-free paint, a formal government recall should still be made for all bottles manufactured with Lead paint prior to the date that any switch was [or will be] made AND we request the the CPSC use their enforcement power to demand that Lansinoh publish a highly visible notice on their website and social media channels alerting the pubic to the fact that their bottles are painted with Lead paint and should not be used, along with (if relevant) a notice informing the public at what date in 2022 they switched to Lead-free paint (if, in fact they took that step in remedying the problem in response to being alerted to [REDACTED]ÃÂs findings of Lead in the paint on their glass baby bottles.)

CHILDREN IMPACTED

In the CPSCÃÂs current violation report form there is not a place or way to note that it is not possible to know how many children have been impacted by this particular violation. The only choice is to select that a specific child has been impacted or that no children have been impacted. We respectfully request that you change this form so it is easy to select the option that it is LIKELY that children have been impacted, but not confirmed. This should be considered to be the case with all CPSIA violations that are related to Lead paint on childrenÃÂs products. Any amount of Lead exposure is too much. Lead paint is the most likely source of Lead exposure for children. Children are not lab rats. The amount of Lead exposure caused by a specific product (in the context of other potential Lead exposure in a childÃÂs life) may not be measurable as an isolated quantifiable number by current blood Lead testing typically available in most clinics and hospitals - however the concern is not for a specific incidental exposure caused by a specific product. The concern is for a childrenÃÂs product that is painted with lead paint contributing to total aggregate Lead exposure in a childÃÂs life - which can add up to measurable levels and specific significant impacts - whether or not it was known that the child was definitively impacted by that particular product at the time of exposure.

incident_description:
Our complaint involves the Dr. BrownÃÂs Natural FlowÃÂ® Deluxe Baby Bottle Sterilizer, model #AC045 / serial number 21164-27786-02122. The Instructions for Use (IFU) contain inadequate instructions. IFU includes both the printed and online version as of the date of this complaint. This product is used to sterilize infant feeding items and accessories. The set includes a lift-out basket, tongs, and a measuring cup.

The reason for our complaint: 

On multiple occasions, "soot" and an excessive amount of black particles were found inside the machine and inside Dr. Brown's baby bottle vents after use. 

To that end, we have noted the following deficiencies in the labeling material:

The IFU instructs the user to wash, rinse and empty the baby bottles and accessories before running the appliance but does not specifically instruct the user to dry, or air-dry, the items before running the appliance. Drying the bottles prior to running the appliance allows for the removal of residual water leftover from the dishwasher or rinsing process. Residual water left on the outside and/or inside of the bottles and accessories may contaminate the distilled water used to sterilize the bottles, especially if city water is not properly filtered or is hard water, and may exacerbate the build-up of mineral deposits on the heating element surface.

IFU does not specifically instruct the user to visually inspect inside Dr. BrownÃÂs baby bottle vents. Regardless if any foreign matter tested harmless, it is to be expected that baby bottles do not contain foreign particles inadvertently trapped inside Dr. Brown's bottle vents from either the cleaning process or after using the Dr. Brown's sterilizer. 

The IFU does not specifically instruct the user to stop using the appliance when mineral deposits are present.

The IFU does not instruct the user to re-wash bottles and accessories if black flakes and/or residue is found on the lift-out basket and heating element after using the appliance. 

As previously noted, the IFU states, "CAUTION:DO NOT EXCEED the recommended amount of water. If it is necessary to drain water from the base, always POUR AWAY FROM YOU". We believe this statement does not provide a sufficient caution against leaving residual water to pool on the heating element after a cycle is finished. It is common to have a small volume of water left in the steriliser after a completed cycle. IFU for model AC045 does not instruct the user to empty out any remaining water once the cycle finishes and wipe down all surfaces after each use. Water left inside the machine may exacerbate the build-up of mineral deposits/limescale.

The IFU states, "Before running this appliance, it is important that all bottles, bottle parts and/or other accessories are clean. They must be washed, rinsed and empty." IFU does not provide a warning to dry all the items prior to using the sterilizer. It is well-known that plastic baby bottle components don't retain heat well and may have residual water droplets on the outside from the dishwasher drying cycle. Dishwashers use city water, therefore, any water droplets leftover from the drying cycle will most likely exacerbate the build-up of hard-water deposits on the machine.

The "Instructions For Use" states, "Before running this appliance, it is important that all bottles, bottle parts and/or other accessories are clean. They must be washed, rinsed and empty." At the time of this complaint, we believe the IFU does not provide a sufficient warning to the user to visually inspect baby bottles, bottle parts, and accessories for foreign matter prior to using the sterilizer. A great number of users may be under the assumption that everything that comes out of a dishwasher is clean and rinsed. However, it is not uncommon for debris to get stuck on caps, bottle vents, and nipples.
justification: The incident involves inadequate instructions leading to potential contamination but no reported injury or death.

incident_description:
What happened that made you want to report? 

We narrowly escaped significant injury when my 12-month old daughter managed to climb out of her lobster high chair (the type that attaches to a table top) and onto our counter height kitchen table. Had I not been mere feet away grabbing something from the fridge when I noticed her nearly entirely on the kitchen table, she could have been significantly injured. I emailed the company and included pictures of the incident and my daughter in the high chair to see if they could help advise on the situation, but have not heard back in a couple of days. I mentioned the incident to a friend tonight and she responded that the exact same thing happened to them and she felt it was so risky and they discontinued using the product. With this apparently being a common issue, I think this warrants a closer inspection of the safety features of this product.

What type of product(s) were being used?

A Phil&Teds lobster highchair attached to a kitchen table. It was attached to a sturdy table top of a counter height kitchen table per the instructions that came with the product.

Who was using the product(s)?

My 12-month old daughter who currently weighs 17lbs and 5oz.

How were the product(s) being used?

According to the manual as best as I can tell. My daughter was in the high chair with the shoulder straps tightened to the best of my abilities. There is no chest clip and the shoulder straps are loosely  attached to horizontal straps at the bottom. This means the lower attachment can freely slide some inches back and forth, making it impossible to tighten them enough to have a determined baby unable to wiggle their arms out of the shoulder straps. Since there is no hip strap either, this leaves the infant entirely unsecured in the seat. At the time of the incident, I had gotten up from the kitchen table to grab something from the fridge. Our fridge is only about 6 feet from the kitchen table. I grabbed a cupcake from the refrigerator shelf and placed it onto the kitchen table out of my daughter's reach. I went back to the fridge to retrieve a second cupcake, which I'm estimating took me maybe 15seconds total. In this timeframe my daughter managed to twist her body sideways far enough to slip both arms out of the shoulder straps and pull her left leg through the leg hole onto the seat portion of the high chair. From there, she pulled herself forward with her arms on the table top and used her left leg pushing off of the seat to pull her right leg out of the second leg hole. By the time I realized what was going on and managed to close the 6 foot gap from the fridge to the table she had her first knee on the kitchen table and was starting to crawl towards the cupcake.

Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product?

The only thing that prevented a potentially catastrophic injury due to falling off of our counter height kitchen table was me being mere feet away and sprinting back to the table to grab her. Since falls are a leading cause of emergency room visits in infants and toddlers, I believe this had a significant injury risk.

How did any injuries occur?
They were narrowly avoided.

Additional information
I searched the manufacturers website when trying to look into whether I failed to properly use the safety straps on the high chair (there is nothing like a chest clip that secures the shoulder straps and prevents the child from merely pulling their arm free). That's when I came across the description of a "5-point safety harness" on the website. I'm really not sure I would describe the straps as a 5-point harness system, since there is no chest or crotch buckle that actually secures the shoulder straps to prevent the infant from merely sliding them off their shoulders. The hip tightening strap loops through the piece on the front that creates the leg openings. This means it does not actually tighten around the infant. The shoulder straps further cannot be securely tightened since the bottom connection loosely ties onto a horizontal strap. This means it can slide back and forth at minimum a few inches, which prevents them from being tightened to where an infant would be unable to merely slip them off.
justification: The incident involved a near-miss with potential for significant injury, but no actual injury occurred.

incident_description: I purchased the Halo Bassinest Flex sleeper for my newborn.  This bassinest is rated for infants up to 20lbs or 5 months of age. Having done research on this product I have found multiple reviews on different distributors of this product ([REDACTED], Buy Buy Baby,
etc.) with the same issue as mine where the supporting legs pop out when in use. I believe that these reviews are also due to the fact that they had two "front" bases included in their package. Like previously mentioned if someone was to not see both bases labeled as "Front" they would assume the walker is properly assembled. Due to the inability of this company to consistently include the proper parts in the box I believe a recall should be issued. A child using this product could get seriously injured or killed due to the wrong base being using in assembly. I have documentation of my incident, as well as the documentation from the company. Since other people have had the same issue I think this needs to be investigated further to avoid a worse case scenario of a child being killed using this product. incident_description:
I bought a Cosco Simple Fold High Chair on 8/23/2021 to replace an older high chair for my toddler. Immediately, I noticed the seat had a deep recline that could not be adjusted. I was constantly adjusting my child during meals, and she was having a hard time with gagging during meals when she hadn't before. She has had 2 almost choking incidents and ended up actually choking while in the chair since purchase and has never choked before. There is a MAJOR difference between gagging and choking. No doubt had everything to do with the improper reclining position of the chair.

On the morning she actually choked, I gave her the same breakfast she's eaten a million times, and I was right there watching her like a hawk as always. She took a bite, swallowed, and I saw the fear in her eyes when it got stuck. I thought for sure she'd gag it up, but she didn't. Her face turned red then almost purple in an instant. She tried to cough or cry and couldn't. I knew she was in trouble. She was so far leaned back she couldn't pull herself up and started clawing at the tray trying. All of this happened in a matter of like 3 seconds. I was already pulling the tray off then pushed her forward so her belly hit the little bar first (like a heimlich move) while my other hand was reaching for the buckles, and thankfully that was enough to dislodge the food. She projectile vomited, gasped for air, and started screaming which at that point was the most amazing sound in the world to me. This happened in under 20-30 seconds, and I was right there. What if I wasn't? She was completely silent until the food was dislodged. She would have been choking in silence until I happened to notice my child was blue. If you know eating safety for babies and toddlers, you know that position is absolutely important when it comes to preventing choking. How many children have been potentially hurt by this high chair? Or maybe even killed? What if I hadn't been attentive or was distracted by my other child this morning? Many parents just put their children in high chairs with food while they do other tasks. This high chair is dangerous for older babies and toddlers. It scares me to think what could have happened if I wasn't right there to help clear my daughter's airway, or if I didn't know what to do to help a choking child. Most people haven't taken even basic CPR classes.
justification: The child experienced choking incidents due to the high chair's design, requiring immediate intervention to prevent serious harm.

I read several blogs mentioning that cribs manufactured prior to this date are unlikely to meet the new standards and that the only way to find out whether a pre-2011 crib is compliant is to reach out to manufacturer and/or retailer. 

Thus, I reached out to Ikea. On at least 3 separate calls to customer service, I was unable to speak with somebody. One one call, I spoke to a customer service representative who told me the crib was compliant. When I inquired how she knew this, I was informed that "if it were not safe, we would not sell it." She was not privy to any documentation to this effect and refused to put this fact in writing. After insisting on discussing with a manager, I was placed on hold and then disconnected.

I get that this is a tough time, but I am worried that Ikea is compromising safety (of babies no less) in order to deal with their supply chain woes.

incident_description:
Less than 4 months ago, we bought from Target the pressure mounted wooden expandable baby gate from the brand Regalo. The baby gate doesn't require assembly, it comes completely ready to use. It has 4 plastic brackets, each with 1 screw. One of the brackets came loose and our 1-year-old baby swallowed the screw, which is very sharp.

My husband was about 3 feet away from our son, but he didn't realize what he was playing with until our son started to choke. I ran when I heard the choking noise. My husband and I went through a horrific experience trying to help our son to breath, he was chocking severely and stopped breathing. I turned him belly-down and hit his back several times. Luckily he finally got the screw down and started to breath. We then saw the plastic bracket on the floor and realized what it was. We went to check the baby gate to find it was missing a bracket and screw. We knew right then what our son had just swallowed. 

We took him to the emergency room at [REDACTED] Los Angeles. There he had the first of many x-rays. The pediatrician specialist and surgeons were at [REDACTED] Fontana, which is about 1 hour away, so they sent us there in an ambulance. After a very long process and a lot of waiting and x-rays, the surgeons decided that the screw was too far down and could not be removed through the throat. We were admitted to the hospital for observation so the doctors could monitor the progress of the screw through his digestive system. On the next day the surgeons came to the conclusion that the screw was stuck in the large intestine and needed to be surgically removed. 

Our son had the surgery and spent 1 more night at the hospital. He is now recovering well and we are so thankful for the surgeons at [REDACTED]. They did a great operation.

The Regalo baby gate should NOT have had a loose screw after such a short period of time - or ever! We always used the gate as intended by the manufacturer, so we are severely disappointed that the product could have failed after such a short period of use. We have been very traumatized and still healing from this experience. This product should not be available to anyone at this point. We don't want the same to happen to others. It should be recalled.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe injury requiring surgery due to a swallowed screw from a defective baby gate.
